claim: DMS primarily forms three methyl modifications on mRNA: N1-methyladenosine (m1A), N3-methylcytidine (m3C), N7-methylguanosine (m7G).
source: For example, one of the most widely used RNA structure-probing reagents, dimethyl sulfate (DMS), primarily forms three methyl modifications on mRNA: N1-methyladenosine (m1A), N3-methylcytidine (m3C), N7-methylguanosine (m7G) (Lawley and Brookes, 1963; Mustoe et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lawley and Brookes, 1963 and Mustoe et al., 2019

claim: m1A and m3C can be readily detected due to their ability to impair reverse transcription and induce misincorporations in cDNA.
source: Among these, m1A and m3C contain methyl modifications located on the Watson-Crick face and therefore can be readily detected due to their ability to impair reverse transcription and thus induce misincorporations in cDNA (Peattie and Gilbert, 1980; Inoue and Cech, 1985; Lempereur et al., 1985; Wells et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior work demonstrating this property

claim: m7G has minimal effects on reverse transcription.
source: In contrast, m7G has minimal effects on reverse transcription.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge in the field

claim: m7G contains a methyl modification on the Hoogsteen face, rather than the Watson-Crick face of guanosine.
source: Since m7G contains a methyl modification on the Hoogsteen face, rather than the Watson-Crick face of guanosine, it does not efficiently perturb reverse transcription.
evidence: Based on established structural knowledge of m7G

claim: The accessibility of the N7 position of G in RNA cannot be readily assessed.
source: As a result, the accessibility of the N7 position of G in RNA cannot be readily assessed.
evidence: Inferred from the inability of m7G to perturb reverse transcription

claim: RNA secondary structure is mediated by Watson-Crick base pairs and includes the location of helices and loop regions in an RNA structure.
source: RNA secondary structure is mediated by Watson-Crick base pairs and includes the location of helices and loop regions in an RNA structure.
evidence: Standard definition in RNA structural biology

claim: Interactions that occur with the Hoogsteen face have important roles in mediating RNA tertiary structures.
source: In contrast to the Watson-Crick face, interactions that occur with the Hoogsteen face have important roles in mediating RNA tertiary structures.
evidence: Established knowledge about RNA tertiary structure

claim: G-quadruplexes rely on hydrogen bonding interactions of the N7 position of G (N7G).
source: These include G-quadruplexes, which rely on hydrogen bonding interactions of the N7 position of G (N7G) (Gellert et al., 1962).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gellert et al., 1962

claim: G-quadruplexes comprise stacks of two or more G-tetrads, which are square planar arrangements of four guanine bases that interact through hydrogen bonds around a central potassium ion.
source: G-quadruplexes comprise stacks of two or more G-tetrads, which are square planar arrangements of four guanine bases that interact through hydrogen bonds around a central potassium ion (Gellert et al., 1962).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gellert et al., 1962

claim: G-quadruplexes are physiologically important RNA structures associated with translation, splicing, phase separation, and small molecule binding.
source: G-quadruplexes are physiologically important RNA structures associated with translation, splicing, phase separation, and small molecule binding (Roschdi et al., 2022; Marcel et al., 2011; Blice-Baum and Mihailescu, 2014; Zhang et al., 2019b; Asamitsu et al., 2023; Rodriguez et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior work

claim: G-quadruplex folding appears to be dynamically regulated by specific helicases.
source: G-quadruplex folding also appears to be dynamically regulated by specific helicases (Creacy et al., 2008; Guo and Bartel, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Creacy et al., 2008 and Guo and Bartel, 2016

claim: BASH MaP detects DMS-induced modifications on both the Watson-Crick and Hoogsteen faces by using potassium borohydride to convert m7G to an abasic site.
source: BASH MaP detects DMS-induced modifications on both the Watson-Crick and Hoogsteen faces by using potassium borohydride to convert m7G to an abasic site.
evidence: Description of the BASH MaP method developed in this study

claim: The abasic site resulting from m7G conversion is detected by a specific signature misincorporation during reverse transcription.
source: The resulting abasic site is detected by a specific signature misincorporation during reverse transcription.
evidence: Description of the BASH MaP method

claim: m7G can be selectively converted to an abasic site by reduction with potassium borohydride and heating in an acidic buffer.
source: Previous studies showed that m7G can be selectively converted to an abasic site, which is an efficient inducer of misincorporations (Küpfer et al., 2007). In this reaction, m7G is reduced with potassium borohydride (Zhang et al., 2022) and then converted to an abasic site by heating in an acidic buffer (Enroth et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2019a; Figure 1a).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work and shown in Figure 1a

claim: Treatment of RNA with potassium borohydride (800 mM) for 4 hr at room temperature followed by heating in pH 2.9 buffer for 4 hr at 45 °C induces an average misincorporation rate of 70% at m7G1638 in 18S rRNA.
source: Plots of misincorporations rates revealed that 4 hr of borohydride treatment induced an average misincorporations rate of 70% at G1638.
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 1C

claim: Misincorporations at m7G-derived abasic sites are primarily G→T transitions and G deletions when using SuperScript II reverse transcriptase.
source: The misincorporations were primarily G→T and G deletions when using SuperScript II (Figure 1d).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 1D

claim: Marathon RT produces predominantly G→T transitions with lower deletion rates than SuperScript II at abasic sites.
source: Similar results were seen with Marathon RT, with fewer deletions (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1a

claim: BASH MaP of Spinach RNA produces an average G misincorporation rate of 4.6% compared to 0.58% for DMS MaP and 0.31% for untreated RNA.
source: Notably, BASH-MaP-treated Spinach produced an average G misincorporation rate of 4.6% compared to 0.58% for DMS MaP and 0.31% for untreated RNA (Figure 1e).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 1E

claim: BASH MaP produces highly reproducible measures of DMS reactivity over a range of DMS concentrations (85 mM to 170 mM) with R²=0.9928.
source: In addition to m1A, m3C, and m7G, DMS also forms m1G and m3U to a lesser extent (Mustoe et al., 2019; Mitchell et al., 2023). The misincorporation rates for all four nucleotides were highly correlated between 85 mM and 170 mM DMS (R2=0.9928) with a high Pearson correlation coefficient over a range of DMS concentrations (Figure 1f and Figure 1—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 1F and Figure 1—figure supplement 1b

claim: The reduction and depurination steps of BASH MaP do not compromise the detection of methylated A, C, and U.
source: Notably, the misincorporation rate of A, C, and U bases remained correlated between the two samples (Figure 1g and Figure 1—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 1G and Figure 1—figure supplement 1b

claim: BASH MaP accurately discriminates between single-stranded and base-paired A, C, and U bases with AUC values of 0.87, 1.0, and 0.81 respectively.
source: Panels (H–J) demonstrate that BASH MaP accurately discriminates between single-stranded and base-paired A, C, and U bases.
evidence: ROC curve analysis shown in Figure 1H-J

claim: Single-stranded G's in Spinach display high misincorporation rates in BASH MaP.
source: Each of these three G's displayed a high misincorporation rate (Figure 2b).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 2B

claim: G's in G-quadruplexes show the lowest misincorporation rates in Spinach BASH MaP.
source: Notably, the G's constituting the RNA G-quadruplex of Spinach showed the lowest misincorporation rates in Spinach (Figure 2c).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 2C

claim: G's that are highly resistant to DMS methylation are likely engaged in hydrogen-bonding interactions involving N7 and may reflect G's within G-quadruplexes.
source: Thus, G's that are highly resistant to DMS methylation are likely engaged in hydrogen-bonding interactions involving N7 and may reflect G's within G-quadruplexes.
evidence: Inference from experimental data on Spinach G-quadruplex

claim: BASH MaP analysis of 15x polyUG repeat RNA reveals low misincorporation rates for nine G's expected to be hydrogen bonded in all four G-quadruplex registers.
source: BASH MaP analysis of the 15 x polyUG repeat RNA revealed low misincorporation rates for the nine G's expected to be hydrogen bonded in all four G-quadruplex registers (G26-G42) (Figure 2e).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 2E

claim: G's that participate in only one G-quadruplex register show the highest misincorporation rates in 15x polyUG repeat RNA.
source: G's that could participate in only one G-quadruplex showed the highest misincorporation rate (Figure 2f).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 2F

claim: N1G reactivity is insufficient to identify G's in a G-quadruplex because it cannot discriminate between base-paired G's and G-quadruplex G's.
source: Using this approach, we observed no discrimination between base-paired G's and G's involved in a G-quadruplex (Figure 2—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1c

claim: N7G reactivity measured by BASH MaP uniquely identifies G's that are involved in a G-quadruplex.
source: Overall, these data suggest that N7G reactivity measured by BASH MaP uniquely identifies G's that are involved in a G-quadruplex.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from comparison of N7G and N1G reactivity data

claim: BASH MaP of AKT2 3'UTR in SH-SY5Y cells identifies G's with low DMS reactivity that map to previously identified in-cell G-quadruplex positions.
source: The normalized reactivity plot reveals N7G protections from DMS at previously identified in cell G-quadruplex G's as well as other G-tracts. Together, these data support the formation of a G-quadruplex in 3'UTR of the AKT2 mRNA in SH-SY5Y cells.
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 2G

claim: BASH MaP produces significantly more misincorporations per RNA molecule than DMS MaP.
source: Analysis of Spinach BASH MaP data indicated significantly more misincorporations per RNA molecule than DMS MaP (Figure 3—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1a

claim: The percentage of reads with two or more misincorporations doubled after BASH MaP, and the average number of total misincorporations per read increased from 1.35 to 2.9.
source: The percentage of reads with two or more misincorporations doubled after BASH MaP, and the average number of total misincorporations per read increased from 1.35 to 2.9 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1b–c).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1b-c

claim: BASH-MaP-treated Spinach produces G-G correlations between G's comprising the G-quadruplex.
source: In contrast, BASH-MaP treated Spinach produced G – G correlations between G's comprising the G-quadruplex (Figure 3e).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 3E

claim: Network analysis of BASH MaP G-G co-occurring misincorporations reveals that G-quadruplex G's form a distinct cluster.
source: The smaller cluster was composed of seven G nucleotides, with six of them forming part of the Spinach G-quadruplex and mixed tetrad (Figure 3g).
evidence: Network analysis shown in Figure 3G

claim: G's engaged in canonical base pairs contribute to the stability of nearby base-paired G's.
source: These results reveal that G's engaged in canonical base pairs contribute to the stability of nearby base-paired G's.
evidence: Inference from network analysis of G-G correlations

claim: Network analysis of AKT2 BASH MaP data identifies four connected and lowly reactive G's that likely form a G-quadruplex.
source: The network formed four main clusters, one of which contained four connected and lowly reactive G's (Figure 3—figure supplement 2b).
evidence: Network analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2b

claim: The AKT2 3'UTR G-quadruplex may adopt an unusual topology with a long central loop.
source: Analysis of the 10 G-quadruplex conformers with the lowest average misincorporation rate revealed a common large central loop element (Figure 3—figure supplement 2d). Overall, these results further support the formation of a G-quadruplex in the AKT2 3' UTR in cells and suggests the AKT2 3' UTR G-quadruplex may adopt an unusual topology with a long central loop.
evidence: Computational analysis of BASH MaP data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2d

claim: M2 BASH MaP displays unique signals in the mutate-and-map heatmap in the G-quadruplex and P3 region of Spinach.
source: M2 BASH MaP displays unique signals in the mutate-and-map heatmap in the G-quadruplex (red box) and P3 (grey box) region of Spinach.
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 4A-B

claim: PCR-derived mutations at any G-quadruplex G cause increased N7G methylation in all G-quadruplex tetrad layers.
source: However, a zoomed-in plot of the Spinach M2 BASH MaP heatmap indicated that a mutation installed during PCR in any G-quadruplex G caused increased N7G methylation in all G-quadruplex tetrad layers (Figure 4d).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 4D

claim: G-quadruplex folding is easily perturbed by changing any G in the G-quadruplex.
source: Therefore, M2 BASH MaP revealed that G-quadruplex folding is easily perturbed by changing any G in the G-quadruplex.
evidence: Inference from M2 BASH MaP data

claim: N7G reactivity is highly influenced by local base stacking interactions.
source: Therefore, local distortions of base stacking caused by PCR-derived mutations may explain the novel signals present in the Spinach M2 BASH MaP heatmap. Together, these data further suggest that N7G reactivity is highly influenced by local base stacking interactions.
evidence: Inference from M2 BASH MaP heatmap analysis

claim: Incorporation of tertiary-folding constraints from BASH MaP through DAGGER enables accurate secondary structure modeling of Spinach.
source: Application of DAGGER to the BASH MaP Spinach dataset produced a consensus secondary structure that closely resembled the crystallographic secondary structure (Figure 5d).
evidence: Computational modeling results shown in Figure 5D

claim: The DAGGER secondary structure model of Spinach includes a properly formed P1, P2, and P3 stem and is devoid of false helical regions.
source: The resulting secondary structure model included a properly formed P1, P2, and P3 stem and was devoid of false helical regions (Figure 5d).
evidence: Computational modeling results shown in Figure 5D

claim: DANCE analysis of Spinach M2 BASH MaP data identifies two states with abundances of 80.6% and 19.4%.
source: DANCE identified two conformations denoted as State 1 and State 2 of 80.6% and 19.4% abundance.
evidence: DANCE deconvolution results shown in Figure 6A

claim: DANCE deconvolution of Spinach BASH MaP without PCR-derived mutations produces two states with abundances of 78.7% and 21.3%.
source: DANCE deconvolution of this dataset also produced two states with abundances of 78.7% and 21.3% which closely resembles the abundances seen in the DANCE deconvolution of the M2 BASH MaP dataset (Figure 6—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: DANCE deconvolution results shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1a

claim: State 1 and State 2 of Spinach differ in the core and P2 domains but remain unchanged in stems P1 and P3.
source: The plot of change in reactivity shows that State 1 and State 2 differ in the core and P2 domains but remain unchanged in stems P1 and P3.
evidence: Reactivity difference analysis shown in Figure 6B

claim: G-quadruplex G's in Spinach State 1 display strong protections from DMS methylation.
source: G-quadruplex G's in State 1 displayed strong protections from DMS methylation (Figure 6d).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 6D

claim: G-quadruplex G's in Spinach State 2 display reactivity to DMS like base paired G's.
source: In contrast, G-quadruplex G's in State 2 were found to display reactivity to DMS like base paired G's (Figure 6e).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 6E

claim: Single stranded A's in the G-quadruplex loops show decreased reactivity to DMS in Spinach State 2.
source: Analysis of single stranded A's in the G-quadruplex loops showed an opposite trend with decreased reactivity to DMS in State 2 (Figure 6g).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 6G

claim: The misfolded Spinach adopts an alternative conformation characterized by a breakdown of N7G hydrogen bonding in the G-quadruplex core.
source: Together, these results suggest that the misfolded Spinach adopts an alternative conformation characterized by a breakdown of N7G hydrogen bonding in the G-quadruplex core.
evidence: Inference from DANCE deconvolution data

claim: Mutation of two single stranded loop A's to C's in Spinach results in ~40% of wildtype fluorescence.
source: Surprisingly, mutation of two single stranded loop A's to C's resulted in ~40% of the wildtype fluorescence (Figure 6h).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 6H

claim: Mutation of three loop A's to C's in Spinach results in near complete loss of fluorescence.
source: Mutation of three loop A's to C's resulted in near complete loss of fluorescence (Figure 6h).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 6H

claim: DAGGER analysis of Spinach BASH MaP data identifies two major clusters with alternative base pairing in the P2 domain.
source: The key difference between the representative secondary structure of Cluster 1 and the representative secondary structure of Cluster 2 involved alternative base-pair interactions in the P2 domain (Figure 5—figure supplement 1a–b).
evidence: DAGGER clustering results shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1a-b

claim: Broccoli contains sequence differences from Spinach concentrated in the P2 domain that stabilize the fluorescent conformation.
source: However, sequence differences in Spinach which led to the improved Broccoli aptamer are concentrated in the P2 domain (Figure 6—figure supplement 1b). In Spinach, a non-canonical A•A base pair just below the mixed tetrad was present as a G•C pair in Broccoli. Additionally, another non-canonical U•U base pair in Spinach was present as an A•U base pair in Broccoli. These sequence differences are expected to enhance folding of the fluorescent conformation by stabilizing the P2 domain.
evidence: Structural comparison shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1b

claim: The non-fluorescent conformation of Spinach involves the G-quadruplex G's forming an extended P3 domain characterized by base-pairing with loop residues and a reorganization of the P2 domain.
source: Together, these results suggest that the non-fluorescent conformation of Spinach involves the G-quadruplex G's forming an extended P3 domain characterized by base-pairing with loop residues and a reorganization of the P2 domain.
evidence: Inference from multiple lines of experimental data

claim: BASH MaP expands the structures that can be detected using DMS-based structure probing methods.
source: Thus, BASH MaP expands the structures that can be detected using DMS-based structure probing methods.
evidence: Summary conclusion from all experimental results

claim: The N7 position of G is the most nucleophilic site in RNA and therefore the most reactive atom in RNA for DMS methylation.
source: In principle, the accessibility of N7G can be readily assessed because the N7 position of G is the most nucleophilic site in RNA and therefore the most reactive atom in RNA for DMS methylation (Lawley and Brookes, 1963).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lawley and Brookes, 1963

claim: Abasic sites are efficient inducers of misincorporations during reverse transcription.
source: Previous studies showed that m7G can be selectively converted to an abasic site, which is an efficient inducer of misincorporations (Küpfer et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Küpfer et al., 2007

claim: The 18S ribosomal RNA from HeLa cells contains a stoichiometric m7G at position 1638.
source: To test this, we used the 18 S ribosomal RNA (rRNA) from HeLa cells, which contains a stoichiometric m7G at position 1638 (Piekna-Przybylska et al., 2008; Choi and Busch, 1978; Haag et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work

claim: The crystal structure of Spinach revealed a non-canonical G-quadruplex, G's in helices, as well as G's not involved in structural interactions.
source: The crystal structure of Spinach revealed a non-canonical G-quadruplex, G's in helices, as well as G's not involved in structural interactions (Huang et al., 2014; Warner et al., 2014; Fernandez-Millan et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to crystal structure studies

claim: The N7G of each G in the Spinach G-quadruplex participates in Hoogsteen-face hydrogen-bonding interactions with an adjacent G.
source: The N7G of each G in the G-quadruplexes participates in Hoogsteen-face hydrogen-bonding interactions with an adjacent G and is thus expected to be inaccessible to DMS.
evidence: Based on known G-quadruplex structure

claim: Most G's in helices exhibit reduced misincorporation rates compared to G's in single-stranded regions.
source: In contrast, most G's in helices exhibited reduced misincorporation rates compared to G's in single-stranded regions (Figure 2b).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 2B

claim: The reduced methylation of helical G's is consistent with low accessibility of the major groove in duplex RNA.
source: Although helical G's do not have hydrogen-bonds at the N7 position, the reduced methylation of helical G's is consistent with low accessibility of the major groove in duplex RNA (Weeks and Crothers, 1993).
evidence: Supported by citation to Weeks and Crothers, 1993

claim: Base-paired G's at helix termini exhibit enhanced major groove accessibility.
source: These G's are located at helix termini, a location previously shown to exhibit enhanced major groove accessibility, and in locations of unusual base stacking (Weeks and Crothers, 1993).
evidence: Supported by citation to Weeks and Crothers, 1993

claim: The 15x polyUG repeat RNA can theoretically form four unique G-quadruplexes composed of 12 consecutive GU repeats.
source: We choose a UG repeat length of 15 because we reasoned that this repeat length could theoretically form four unique G-quadruplexes composed of 12 consecutive GU repeats (Figure 2c).
evidence: Theoretical prediction shown in Figure 2C-D

claim: Register 2 of the 15x polyUG G-quadruplex displays the lowest average misincorporation rate and marks the most abundant register.
source: Interestingly, a plot of the average misincorporation rate for each register revealed that the propensity to form each register was not equal (Figure 2—figure supplement 1b). Instead, the G-quadruplex in register 2, which starts at G22 and ends at G44, displayed the lowest average misincorporation rate and therefore marks the most abundant register (Figure 2—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1b

claim: The reactivity of N1G is between 10- and 100-fold lower than N7G, even under higher pH conditions which promote the formation of m1G.
source: Compared to the N7G, we found the reactivity of N1G is between 10- and 100-fold lower, even under higher pH conditions which promote the formation of m1G (Mustoe et al., 2019; Mitchell et al., 2023; Figure 2—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1c

claim: Most G-quadruplexes in mRNAs are globally unfolded in HEK293T and HeLa mammalian cell lines.
source: Despite their low resolution, these methods have suggested that most G-quadruplexes in mRNAs are globally unfolded in HEK293T and HeLa mammalian cell lines (Guo and Bartel, 2016; Kharel et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work

claim: A small subset of G-quadruplexes remain folded in cells, including one in the 3'UTR of the AKT2 mRNA.
source: Although most G-quadruplexes are unfolded, a small subset of G-quadruplexes appeared to remain folded in cells. One of these folded G-quadruplexes resides in the 3' UTR of the AKT2 mRNA (Guo and Bartel, 2016; Figure 2—figure supplement 1f).
evidence: Supported by citation to Guo and Bartel, 2016

claim: The misincorporations at G's in AKT2 reflect formation of m7G since they exhibit the characteristic G→T and G deletion misincorporation signature.
source: Notably, the misincorporations at G's in AKT2 reflect formation of m7G since they exhibited the characteristic G→T and G deletion misincorporation signature of m7G in BASH MaP (Figure 2—figure supplement 1e).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1e

claim: During RNA breathing, a transient local unfolding event can lead to methylation of an otherwise inaccessible nucleotide.
source: During RNA breathing, a transient local unfolding event can lead to methylation of an otherwise inaccessible nucleotide. The methylated nucleotide can no longer interact with its cognate nucleotide partner, which leads to methylation of the nucleotide partner as well.
evidence: Established mechanism in RNA structure probing

claim: Watson-Crick base pairs have been identified in cells using statistical analysis of misincorporations co-occurring in individual sequencing reads.
source: By using a statistical analysis of misincorporations co-occurring in individual sequencing reads, with each read representing a unique RNA molecule (Homan et al., 2014), Watson-Crick base pairs have been identified in cells (Mustoe et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work

claim: DMS-MaP-treated Spinach displayed strong correlations between A's in the P2 domain and G-quadruplex G residues but displayed no correlations between G-quadruplex G's.
source: DMS-MaP-treated Spinach displayed strong correlations between A's in the P2 domain and G-quadruplex G residues but displayed no correlations between G-quadruplex G's (Figure 3d).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 3D

claim: G-quadruplex G's can be discovered using BASH MaP and produce a specific signature in the RING MaP heatmap.
source: Thus, G-quadruplex G's can be discovered using BASH MaP, in contrast to DMS MaP and produce a specific signature in the RING MaP heatmap.
evidence: Conclusion from RING MaP analysis

claim: Three G-quadruplex G's (G50, G51, and G89) in Spinach did not display co-occurring misincorporations with other G's.
source: Notably, three G-quadruplex G's: G50, G51, and G89, were not represented in the network because they did not display co-occurring misincorporations with other G's.
evidence: Network analysis results

claim: The lack of co-occurring misincorporations at G50, G51, and G89 suggests that methylation of these G's produces an RNA conformation which retains hydrogen bonds at the N7G of other G-quadruplex G's.
source: The lack of co-occurring misincorporations suggests that methylation of G50, G51, and G89 produces an RNA conformation which retains hydrogen bonds at the N7G of other G-quadruplex G's.
evidence: Inference from network analysis

claim: Methylation of even a single N7G within Spinach can lead to global destabilization of RNA structure.
source: The mechanism for these co-occurring methylations is unclear but suggests that methylation of even a single N7G within Spinach can lead to global destabilization of RNA structure.
evidence: Inference from co-occurring misincorporation patterns

claim: The co-occurring misincorporation network data indicates an unusual G-quadruplex topology where at least one conformation of the AKT2 G-quadruplex involves the first two and last two G tracts of the putative G-quadruplex region.
source: Interestingly, the co-occurring misincorporation network data indicates an unusual G-quadruplex topology where at least one conformation of the AKT2 G-quadruplex involves the first two and last two G tracts of the putative G-quadruplex region (Figure 3—figure supplement 2c).
evidence: Network analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2c

claim: In the mutate-and-map method, mutagenic PCR is used to create a pool of RNAs with PCR-derived mutations at every position along the length of the target RNA.
source: In the mutate-and-map method, mutagenic PCR is used to create a pool of RNAs with PCR-derived mutations at every position along the length of the target RNA.
evidence: Description of established method

claim: M2 DMS MaP primarily detects Watson-Crick base pairs in helical regions in an RNA.
source: However, M2 DMS MaP primarily detects Watson-Crick base pairs in helical regions in an RNA (Rouskin et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rouskin et al., 2014

claim: M2 BASH MaP of Spinach and polyUG RNA shows that a mutation at any G-quadruplex G causes large scale increases in N7G accessibility of all G-quadruplex G's.
source: However, a zoomed-in plot of the Spinach M2 BASH MaP heatmap indicated that a mutation installed during PCR in any G-quadruplex G caused increased N7G methylation in all G-quadruplex tetrad layers (Figure 4d). A similar pattern was seen with M2 BASH MaP analysis of 15 x polyUG RNA (Figure 4—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1b

claim: PCR-derived mutations at G bases in the Spinach and polyUG G-quadruplexes cause large scale increases in N7G accessibility which may reflect global destabilization of the G-quadruplex leading to unfolding.
source: Large scale increases in N7G accessibility due to PCR-derived mutations may reflect global destabilization of the G-quadruplex which leads to unfolding.
evidence: Inference from M2 BASH MaP data

claim: PCR-derived mutations within helices induce local distortions of base-stacking interactions and consequently increased N7G reactivity of nearby G's.
source: The vertical lines in the heatmap suggest that PCR-derived mutations within helices induce local distortions of base-stacking interactions and consequently increased N7G reactivity of nearby G's.
evidence: Inference from M2 BASH MaP heatmap patterns

claim: Incorporation of chemical probing data greatly improves RNA secondary structure modeling for most RNAs.
source: Incorporation of chemical probing data greatly improves RNA secondary structure modeling for most RNAs (Deigan et al., 2009; Mathews et al., 2004; Cordero et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work

claim: Computational algorithms are poor at predicting tertiary structures in RNA, such as G-quadruplexes.
source: Notably, computational algorithms are poor at predicting tertiary structures in RNA, such as G-quadruplexes (Vicens and Kieft, 2022; Sato and Kato, 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work

claim: The original predicted secondary structure of Spinach was largely incorrect since it did not anticipate a G-quadruplex at the core of Spinach.
source: The original predicted secondary structure of Spinach (Paige et al., 2011; Strack et al., 2014) was largely incorrect since it did not anticipate a G-quadruplex at the core of Spinach (Fernandez-Millan et al., 2017; Cheng et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work

claim: Addition of constraints from DMS MaP data does not improve modeling of G-quadruplexes since DMS MaP primarily identifies regions of canonical Watson-Crick base pairs.
source: Addition of constraints from DMS MaP data does not improve modeling of G-quadruplexes since DMS MaP primarily identifies regions of canonical Watson-Crick base pairs (Wells et al., 2000).
